Apple has been pushing to collect a commission on sales made through third-party stores, and its hardline stance has frustrated the judge presiding over the Epic Games case.

The company subsequently submitted a more moderate proposal suggesting lower commission rates, but acknowledged in a new regulatory filing that it may ultimately be unable to collect any commission from such sales at all...

Apple's App Store Commission Battle

Antitrust regulators around the world have raised objections to a single situation: developers have historically only been able to sell iPhone apps and in-app content through Apple's official App Store. This monopoly means that the Cupertino-based company can set its own commission rates, and iPhone developers have no choice but to accept them.

The EU is the first region in the world to force Apple to open up third-party app stores, while a US court has ruled that Apple must allow developers to offer in-app purchases and subscriptions through external payment platforms.

Apple has greatly angered the judge in the US case by charging a 27% commission on in-app content sales, even when the transaction was not processed through the App Store. After deducting approximately 3% in payment processing costs, the actual commission rate Apple collects is exactly the same regardless of whether developers sell through the Apple Store.

The judge said this was clearly an abuse of the spirit of the ruling, while Apple argued that the court had not specified an acceptable commission rate for external sales.

Lower Commission Rates

Apple recently filed a more restrained commission proposal for sales outside the App Store.

  • Standard apps at 15%, currently subject to a 30% in-app purchase (IAP) commission;
  • Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals at 10%;
  • Apps under the Small Business Program at 5%.

The company wants the court to view these compromised rates as reasonable compensation, reflecting the resources it has invested in providing developers with Xcode and other tools to assist with app development.

But acknowledges it may ultimately get nothing

However, while Apple is hoping to be allowed to charge these lower commissions, the company acknowledged in a new regulatory filing that the court may not allow it to collect any commission at all on transactions conducted through third-party app stores and other external platforms. The Financial Times reports:

Analysts say this could lead to the first decline in services revenue, which would in turn affect the company's valuation.
